item.title: Midnight Mimosa Malware Was Built Into Android Phones Before Their Owners Ever Switched Them On
item.description:
Thousands of Android phones in more than 150 countries came out of the box already infected. The owners did nothing wrong. The malware sat in the phone’s own system software, installing apps for two years.

You unpack the phone, switch it on, pick a language and sign in with your Google account. By that moment the malware is already running. It came onto the phone together with Android itself, somewhere between the factory and the shop, and because it is part of the system, the phone treats it as one of its own. It has no uninstall button.

Researchers Adrian Mihai Gozob and Alex Baciu at Bitdefender published the campaign on October 8 and named it Midnight Mimosa. Their own security app, which watches how apps behave on a phone, had flagged an app called com.android.system.lite. The name and the look were those of a core Android component, and it was installing and removing other apps without ever asking the owner.

They found it on thousands of devices in more than 150 countries over roughly two years. Mexico, France and Italy had the most, followed by the United States, Germany, Brazil and Spain. The report gives no total, and I am not going to make one up.

The two models that showed up most are the S200 X, sold under the Doogee brand, and the KINGKONG X from Cubot, both rugged Android phones built on MediaTek chips. Behind those two comes a long list of phones pretending to be something they are not. They call themselves S25 Ultra, S26 Ultra, Note 18 Ultra and i17 Pro Max, and some even report a genuine Samsung model number, on phones that brand never made.

The malware runs with the same rights as Android itself. That means it can put apps on the phone and take them off again, hand out permissions, and run code it downloads from the operators’ servers. The researchers counted at least 32 different apps that it swaps onto phones, dressed up as an app lock, weather apps, a file manager, an icon maker, a tool that pulls text out of photos and audio editors. The app locks have no icon, so the owner never sees them on the home screen. The other apps look like ordinary, working apps.

Right before each install, the malware switches the Play Store off. The researchers believe the point is to keep Google Play Protect, the malware scanner built into Android phones, from looking at what goes in. The new app lands, and the Play Store gets switched back on, after a failed install as well as a successful one. The malware has a backup for that too: as soon as the owner is using the phone, the Play Store comes back on, so nothing looks off. Some versions of the malware go one step further and record Google Play as the place they came from. Open the app details and it looks like you installed it yourself from the store.

All of this is about money. These apps show ads, full screen or laid over whatever is on the display, without the owner touching anything, and the malware clicks on them by itself. A minute after an ad appears, it records that the ad made someone act, what the ad business calls a conversion, while no person touched the ad. Those ad screens block screenshots and screen recordings, with a setting Android calls FLAG_SECURE.

The second income is the phone’s internet connection. One of the hidden apps, an app lock without an icon that calls itself Locket, is built to sign the phone up as a relay, so that other people’s internet traffic passes through it. From then on, a website on the other end sees the owner’s connection instead of the person who sent the traffic. Access like that gets sold, and the researchers write that a bigger botnet earns more. To stay exact: their test phone did sign up, but a correction added later says the server it reached was a sinkhole, taken over to catch this kind of traffic. No traffic went through the phone.

That is what the researchers saw happen. What the malware is able to do goes much further. It gives itself the right to read what is on the screen and tap for the user, a feature Android calls Accessibility. It gives itself access to notifications, which is where your messages and login codes land, and it gets permission to read and write text messages. According to the report, all of it sits ready for the operators the moment they want it, because the malware runs whatever code its servers send down. None of those rights were seen in use. And they do not sit still: Accessibility and notification access get switched on, then off again, over and over.

The malware also sends home the numbers that identify the phone: its IMEI, its Android ID and its MAC address. With them go the SIM country code, the time zone, the model, the Android version and the list of apps the owner installed.

Owners were finding it long before it had a name. On July 2, 2026, the owner of a Cubot KingKong X running Android 16 asked on the XDA forum what com.android.sys.extplv was. His antivirus kept flagging it as malicious. The app called itself System, it asked for access to his text messages, his contacts and his accounts, and Android said it had been installed from Google Play. Within a week others turned up in the same thread with the same app, on phones from both brands.

The owner of a Doogee Fire 3 Ultra found out that it hides. When he plugged the phone into a computer with USB debugging switched on, the way you connect a phone to look inside it, the app removed itself almost straight away. When he unplugged the cable, it was back a few hours later. Deleting it did not hold. Switching it off through ADB held for two days, and then it was switched on again. After a factory reset it came back very quickly.

On August 4 a Cubot owner posted that his Telegram account had been taken over that day. Someone had turned on two-factor authentication on his account and changed the email address, and codes were being requested to move his WhatsApp to another phone. On his phone bill he found that since July 25 his phone had sent around 30 text messages to local numbers, at random times of day, without him typing one. That is one person’s account, and it has not been checked independently. The takeover does fit the access this malware gives itself.

Some phones got it from the maker’s own update. An owner of a Doogee Fire 3 Max traced the infected version back to a software update that arrived through the phone’s own update system. It was DOOGEE-Fire 3 Max-EEA-Android15.0-20260616, 373 MB, released on June 15, 2026, from the update server fota5p.adups.com. On August 5 he wrote that this update was still online. In that version the malware ran as com.android.non.szcz, under the name Android System, the same name as the genuine one.

Cubot gave one of its customers an explanation by email in July. According to the company, a development interface meant only for engineering testing had ended up in the firmware for mass production by mistake, and the cleaned firmware had since passed Google’s security certification. What the researchers took apart is a lot more than a leftover testing interface: 32 rotating apps, ad fraud, a proxy, and the Play Store switched off before each install.

Who put it there is unknown. Firmware on affected phones was signed with certificates that the researchers trace to Shenzhen Zediel Co., Ltd. They are careful about that. The certificate does not prove the company wrote the malware or knew about it, and the malware also turned up on phones without that firmware. It could have gone in at the factory that builds phones for a brand, at the company that puts the software together, at a logistics partner, or further down the chain.

The servers do have a history. Two of them show up in Dr.Web’s records of a click-fraud trojan from late 2025, hidden in copies of popular mobile games, among them a Minecraft-style and a GTA-style game, on Xiaomi’s app store. Those games were clean when they came out and got the malware in later updates. That operation also used a domain that had turned up in Joker malware back in 2021.

The researchers found the same ad-fraud code in 13 apps on Google Play, talking to the same servers. They lack the system rights of the version built into the phones, and the report calls them dangerous all the same. I checked on October 10, and all 13 are still there. Together they have more than 1.4 million downloads, and since Google only shows a minimum, the true number is higher. The biggest is Daily Weather, with more than a million.

This has happened before. In November 2016 the security firm Kryptowire found that the BLU R1 HD, an Android phone sold through Amazon, came with update software from Shanghai Adups Technology. That software sent the full text of the owner’s messages, the contacts, the call history, the IMSI and the IMEI to a server in Shanghai. Text messages and call logs went out at 72-hour intervals. The same software could also install apps remotely.

Antivirus apps let it through, because they trust the software a phone ships with. At the time, the company said it was present in more than 150 countries and regions. Ten years later, the infected Fire 3 Max update came from an adups.com server. The company supplies update servers to phone makers, and nothing in the research shows it put this malware there.

In April 2025 Kaspersky found the Triada trojan built into the firmware of counterfeit phones imitating popular brands, on more than 4,500 devices, with more than $264,000 in cryptocurrency stolen. In June 2025 the FBI warned about BADBOX 2.0: millions of TV boxes, projectors, car screens and digital photo frames, infected before they were sold or during setup, and then rented out as proxies. In February 2026 the same security company found a backdoor called Keenadu in the firmware of Android tablets, and in several cases that firmware arrived through an update carrying a valid signature.

Cubot pushed an update in July for the KingKong 9 and the KingKong X that its customers say removed the app. Doogee told owners the problem was solved with a software update, and its build from July 31, 2026 came out clean on the Fire 3 Max owner’s phone and stayed clean at least until August 24. So if you own one of these phones, install the latest update from the maker first.

Then check what is on it. Switch on USB debugging, connect the phone to your computer and run this straight away:

1

adb shell "pm list packages | grep -E 'system.lite|sys.prot|sys.gmsprot|sys.bcprot|sys.dts|sys.extplv|weiapps|weapps|non.szcz|com.mobile.applock'"

Anything that comes back, you can switch off with:

1

adb shell pm disable-user --user 0 com.android.sys.extplv

using the package name you found. Keep the hiding trick in mind: on some phones the app removes itself as soon as the cable goes in, so an empty result does not prove the phone is clean. And it may not stay off. On the Fire 3 Ultra it switched itself back on after two days.

Another owner found that with the Play Store switched off, the app stopped reinstalling itself, since it comes back through the Play Store. That also stops your other apps from updating, so it is a stopgap.

The researchers say plainly that clearing these phones takes either work on the firmware itself or switching the component off over ADB, and that neither is realistic for most owners. If it keeps coming back after the latest update, the firmware is the problem, and the fix is a clean official firmware or another phone.

If you run Pi-hole, or your router lets you block domains, block api.weatherlive.world and oss.showtimetool.com. The first is where the malware gets its orders and reports its fake clicks, the second is where its modules come from.

And if one of those 13 apps is on your phone, uninstall it:

  • → Daily Weather
  • → CoolWeather
  • → WeatherGo
  • → Lock & Hide
  • → All Deleted Messages Recovery
  • → App Icon DIY
  • → Audify
  • → Wavrge
  • → QuickText Extractor
  • → NoteMaster
  • → QR Pocket
  • → Tap to Translate
  • → Tasky

A phone that calls itself an S25 Ultra or an i17 Pro Max at a fraction of the price is neither a Samsung nor an iPhone, and there is no way to know what software it runs.

You can watch this kind of behavior yourself: put a virtual Android device on your own computer and see with Wireshark which servers it talks to. item.title: Telegram Desktop One Click Account Takeover
item.description:
One click in a Telegram group sent 3 of a victim’s login files to an attacker. The victim opened no file and typed no password. Versions up to 7.2.8 did it, and the hole had been there since 2018.

It starts with an invite. Someone you do not know adds you to a Telegram group, and under Telegram’s default settings that needs no agreement from you. Sitting in that group are a few small text files, and you never open them, but they are already on your disk, because Telegram Desktop downloads files up to 8 MiB in a group on its own, the moment you look at the chat.

Then a normal looking link appears, you click it, and three files that together are your Telegram login leave your machine and land in the attacker’s group. There is no password prompt and no warning, and the second Telegram window that does the work opens and closes too fast to see.

That is the attack from end to end. A researcher who goes by beaksec found the chain behind it and published it on October 3, 2026. It has a name now, CVE-2026-107181, rated 8.1 on the older severity scale and 8.6 on the newer one. It works on versions up to and including 7.2.8, confirmed on Windows.

Two small mistakes make it possible. On their own, neither is a disaster. Lined up, they hand your account to someone else.

Start with what happens when you click a link that belongs to Telegram. Windows sees the tg: in front and looks for the app that registered it. Telegram did, so Telegram gets the link.

If the app is still closed, it starts up, reads the link, and handles it. One process, nothing to pass around.

If Telegram is already open, Windows does not check. It starts a second copy anyway. That second copy has to work out that it is the spare, and it does so by reaching for the first one over a local channel between the two programs on the same machine. That channel has a name, inter-process communication, or IPC.

A channel like that carries text, not whole objects. So the link gets flattened into a line of text, handed over, and rebuilt on the other side. Telegram writes that line in a format of its own: a keyword, the value, and a semicolon to close it. A link to open looks like this on the wire:

1

OPEN:tg://x?a=1;

The running copy reads the line, cuts it at each semicolon, and treats the pieces as separate instructions. That works fine, until a value carries a semicolon of its own. Telegram never escapes that one. So a link built like this:

1

tg://x?a=1;CMD:quit

arrives as two instructions instead of one:

1
2

OPEN:tg://x?a=1
CMD:quit

Text the attacker controls has become a command Telegram runs. That is the first mistake.

The command in that example only quits the app. The one that matters is OPEN:, because OPEN: takes any link, with no filter on what kind it is. And inside Telegram’s own code sits a kind of link the operating system knows nothing about, used only within the app: interpret:.

interpret: reads a small instruction file off the disk and sends the file it names into a chat. Telegram built it years ago to publish its own releases. A script wrote a text file naming the channel and the build to upload, and Telegram did the posting. The instruction file looks like this:

1
2
3
4

from: 1234567890
channel: 1987654321
file: path/to/build.exe
caption: notes

The from: line is the only guard. It checks that the release goes out from the right account. Leave the line out, and the check never runs. The feature shows no confirmation and never checks who is asking. It reads the file and sends it.

Reach interpret: through the unescaped semicolon, and a clicked link can tell Telegram to read a file off your disk and send it to a group the attacker owns:

1

tg://x?a=1;OPEN:interpret:instructions.txt

That feature was never meant for users. It had been sitting in the desktop app since at least December 2018.

For that to work, the attacker needs his instruction file already on your machine, at a path he knows. The automatic download hands him both.

Telegram Desktop saves files from a group straight to one folder. On Windows:

1

C:\Users\<user>\Downloads\Telegram Desktop\

He knows the folder. The one thing he does not know is your Windows user name. He does not need it. interpret: also takes relative paths, counted from Telegram’s own data folder, and from there it steps up a few folders and into Downloads without the name:

1

interpret:../../../Downloads/Telegram Desktop/instructions.txt

So he drops the instruction files into the group, Telegram downloads them for you, and the path is fixed.

One piece is left: getting you to click from outside Telegram. A tg: link tapped inside a Telegram chat is handled by the app itself and never touches that local channel, so there is nothing to inject into.

A web link is different. Telegram has no browser of its own, so an https link opens in your system browser. The attacker sends an ordinary looking https link into the chat, and his own server answers it with a redirect to the crafted tg: link. Depending on your browser, and on whether you have opened Telegram links before, the system may ask once whether to open Telegram, and you have probably clicked yes to that prompt before without thinking.

One instruction file sends one target. To take three files, he posts three instruction files and stacks three commands in the single link:

1
2
3
4

tg://x?a=1
;OPEN:interpret:../../../Downloads/Telegram Desktop/instructions1.txt
;OPEN:interpret:../../../Downloads/Telegram Desktop/instructions2.txt
;OPEN:interpret:../../../Downloads/Telegram Desktop/instructions3.txt

Now, why three, and which three. Telegram keeps your login on disk, encrypted. Opening it uses two keys. A long random key, the DEK, encrypts your data. A second key, the KEK, encrypts only the DEK, and the KEK is built from your local passcode together with a bit of salt stored next to the data.

Telegram Desktop has no passcode unless you set one yourself in the settings, and that is what turns a file read into a break-in. With no passcode set, the KEK is built from an empty value and that salt, and the salt sits in the clear in the same file as the encrypted DEK. Read that one file and you can rebuild the KEK, open the DEK, and from there open the login itself.

The three files he takes are:

  • → key_datas, the salt and the encrypted key
  • → the authorization file, the proof that you are logged in
  • → an index Telegram needs to load it

The folder that holds them carries the same name on each installation, because it comes from a fixed word and not from anything about your machine. Drop the three files into a fresh Telegram on his own computer, start it, and your session opens.

This is the part that catches people who feel covered. It is not a login. He never types your phone number, so no code is sent to your phone. He is never asked for your two-step password, because Telegram asks for that only when someone signs in, and he is not signing in. 1

OPEN:tg://x?a=1;

1

tg://x?a=1;CMD:quit

1
2

OPEN:tg://x?a=1
CMD:quit

3
4

item.title: Keurig Smart Coffee Makers Have a Camera Inside and Keurig Wrote It Into Its Privacy Policy in (2020)
item.description:
1,008 GB in 10 days from one coffee maker on a home network. 100 times what it took in. It only had to make coffee. Keurig’s policy says these brewers have a camera inside, and has since 2020.

On October 6, a man who goes by Nomad on X opened the network dashboard he keeps for his parents’ house. He has worked in IT for more than ten years and now works at Prusa, the 3D printer maker. He looks after their network from a distance, and the system he uses for that, UniFi, shows how much data each device in the house sends and receives.

One line stood out. A device called Keurig-20CE2A28C5CE, the Keurig K-Supreme SMART his parents own. In 10 days and 9 hours it had sent 1,008.45 GB and received 9.94 GB.

Received is what comes in, like a film, an update or a web page. Sent is what a device pushes out. This coffee maker sent about a hundred times more than it received. That is about 97 GB a day, or roughly 9 megabits per second, day and night, from a machine that makes coffee.

He unplugged it, posted the screenshot and said his parents were getting a new coffee maker. The post passed 2.4 million views.

Later that day he looked closer. Most of that traffic never left the house. It went onto the home network and not out to the internet, and he thinks it was a bug in that one unit. It still filled up the WiFi access point the coffee maker was connected to, the box that the wireless devices in the house talk to.

The brewer already sat on a separate network for smart devices, often called an IoT network, apart from the laptops and phones. He thought about capturing its packets to see what was inside them, but chose to keep it offline. A device that can flood a network like that, he wrote, is not worth keeping connected.

Keurig had not responded in public by the time of writing. He never captured that traffic, so what was inside the terabyte is still unknown.

Keurig’s privacy policy, in effect since February 13, 2026, spells out what the coffee maker is built to collect. It covers the company’s website and app, and also what it calls its Internet connected devices, the smart brewers.

For those brewers, Keurig collects your usage history: which drink, what size and how strong. Then comes this sentence:

“These brewers also include a camera designed to collect an image of the area where a pod is positioned within the brewer.”

According to the policy, some connected features need that camera. Keurig may also use it for diagnostics, to check that the brewer works properly.

The same part of the policy lists what Keurig picks up from the device you use for its services. Your IP address, a device ID, advertising IDs, your operating system, its software version and your time zone are in there. So is information about your wireless and mobile connection, like your service provider and how strong your signal is.

The feature that has to know which pod is in the brewer is called BrewID, although the policy does not tie the camera to it by name.

BrewID came out on July 27, 2021, with the K-Supreme Plus SMART, at 199.99 dollars. Once the brewer is on WiFi, it recognizes the brand and roast of the K-Cup pod you put in and sets the brew to what the roaster recommends. Keurig says that works for more than 900 pod varieties.

It also keeps count. It tracks how many pods you use, and with Auto-Delivery it orders new ones before you run out.

The brewer only joins a home network on 2.4 GHz with WPA2-PSK, the ordinary WiFi with a single password.

Further down is a section that privacy law asks for, where “sold” and “shared” are legal terms. In it, Keurig Dr Pepper, the company behind Keurig, lists what it has sold or shared for analytics and for ads aimed at you:

  • → Identifiers and contact information
  • → Location, not precise
  • → Internet and electronic activity
  • → Profile inferences, the conclusions a company draws about you from your data

For each of those four, the policy names the same receivers: third party advertisers, data analytics providers and the company’s own affiliates, the other companies in its group.

The policy also says Keurig may use outside analytics and tracking tools, and it names Google Analytics. Those tools help Keurig, or the companies behind them, show you more targeted ads, on Keurig’s own services and across the internet.

That list covers all of Keurig’s services together, so the policy does not say whether anything from the coffee maker itself is part of it.

The app says more. Its page on Apple’s App Store lists six types of data that may be used to track you: purchases, contact info, search history, browsing history, identifiers and usage data.

Tracking has a strict meaning in that store. It means linking what an app collects about you or your device with data from apps and websites owned by other companies, for targeted ads or to measure ads. Sharing that data with a data broker, a company that collects information about people and sells it on, counts too.

Ten types of data are linked to your identity, which means tied to you through your account, your device or other details. Next to those six, the ten include financial info, location, user content and diagnostics.

The camera is not new. I went back through archived copies of the privacy policy. The version that took effect on January 1, 2020 does not mention a camera. The next one, in effect from July 1, 2020, does. The wording was more careful then. The smart brewers “may also include” a camera, and it “may be required” for some services.

The K-Supreme Plus SMART came out with BrewID on July 27, 2021. Keurig wrote the camera into its privacy policy a year before that brewer was on sale.

By the version that took effect on May 8, 2023, both of those mays were gone. Since then the policy says these brewers include a camera, and that it is required.

The version that took effect on January 27, 2022 has something else in it. Its section for California residents opens with this sentence: “At Keurig Dr Pepper, we do not sell your data.” A few lines further down, the same section lists what the company sold in the previous 12 months, for ads aimed at you. Identifiers, geolocation, internet activity and profile inferences went to third party advertisers and to its own affiliates.

The policy explains the gap itself: under California law, a sale also covers the way the company shares limited customer information among its affiliates.

By May 2023, the sentence about not selling your data was gone. The list is still there in the current version, now as sold or shared, with data analytics providers added to the receivers.

The man who found the terabyte also called the brewer DRM waiting to be switched on, a lock that could force you onto official Keurig pods. He did not explain where that came from, but Keurig has done this before, and the lock was broken the same year.

In 2014, Keurig launched the Keurig 2.0. Those brewers ran software that only accepted pods licensed by Keurig. The check sat in the lid. The Boston Globe described a built-in infrared sensor that looked for an invisible ink printed on the foil lid. A pod without that ink got a message on the screen: “Oops! This pack wasn’t designed for this brewer.”

The My K-Cup, a reusable pod you filled with your own coffee, was dropped from the line.

Keurig’s own side used another word. In August 2014, a spokesperson for Green Mountain Coffee Roasters, then the parent company of Keurig, said each Keurig 2.0 brewer would have a camera that can “read” a proprietary taggant material. That is a hidden marker, she said, “embedded on the lid of each Keurig brand pack.” The two descriptions differ, and both are about the same job: seeing which pod is in the brewer.

On December 9, 2014, Kenneth Buckler of Caffeine Security posted an advisory, a public warning about a security hole, on Full Disclosure, a mailing list where researchers publish flaws. He called it the Keurig 2.0 Genuine K-Cup Spoofing Vulnerability. The brewer checked the lid, but it did not check whether that lid had been used before.

So the attack was a used lid. Brew a genuine pod, peel its foil lid off in one piece and keep it. Put a pod from another brand in the brewer, lay the saved lid on top with the puncture hole lined up, close the brewer, and it brews. He gave the flaw a severity score of 4.9 out of 10.

In May 2015, the company reported that sales of brewers and accessories had fallen 23 percent in a quarter. On the call with investors, CEO Brian Kelley said Keurig had underestimated how much people cared about the reusable pod, and that taking it away had been wrong. He said it would come back.

Back in February 2014, TreeHouse Foods filed an antitrust suit against Keurig in New York, a case about unfair control of a market. From March 2014, 27 class actions with similar claims followed, lawsuits filed for a whole group of buyers at once. In July 2020, Keurig agreed to pay 31 million dollars to settle with one group of them: buyers who got their Keurig products through stores and other sellers instead of from Keurig directly.

In 2014, Keurig talked about a camera that reads the lid. Today its own policy says the smart brewers have a camera aimed at the pod, and nothing in that policy or on the product pages says it is used to block pods.

Keurig brewers stood in about 40 million US households, according to the company’s own numbers from February 2024.

You can check for yourself what a smart device in your own house sends, by letting it connect through a machine you control. On a Linux laptop with WiFi, NetworkManager can turn the laptop into a hotspot, its own small WiFi network.

Keurig’s smart brewers need a 2.4 GHz network, so set the band to bg, which is the 2.4 GHz setting. Replace wlan0 with the name of your WiFi card; nmcli device shows it:

1

nmcli device wifi hotspot ifname wlan0 ssid smart-test band bg password "choose-a-long-password"

Connect the device to that network. Then capture its traffic with tshark, the command line version of Wireshark, and filter on the device’s MAC address, the hardware address you find in your router or in the device’s own network settings:

1

sudo tshark -i wlan0 -f "ether host aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff" -w smartdevice.pcap

Let it run for a while and stop it with Ctrl+C. The content of the connections stays encrypted, but two things stay readable. Before a device opens a connection, it looks up the name of the server it wants to reach. When the encrypted connection starts, it says that name again. Those are the DNS lookup and the Server Name Indication, or SNI, and together they show who the device talks to:

1
2

tshark -r smartdevice.pcap -Y "dns.flags.response == 0" -T fields -e dns.qry.name | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
tshark -r smartdevice.pcap -Y "tls.handshake.extensions_server_name" -T fields -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Do this only with your own devices, on your own network.

What you can do:

  • → Open your router or mesh app and look at the data per device; that is where this one showed up
  • → Put smart devices like a coffee maker or a TV on a separate guest or IoT network, away from your laptop and phone
  • → If you never use the Keurig app, there is no reason to keep the brewer on WiFi
  • → In the US, use the “Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information” link at the bottom of keurig.com
  • → On an iPhone, open the App Privacy part of an app’s store page before you install it
  • → Before you buy a smart appliance, read the part of its privacy policy about connected devices; that is where Keurig put the camera

Want to know what your own smart devices send? Run a hotspot, capture with Wireshark and read the server names they look up. item.title: Danfoss Supermarket Fridges Hacked
item.description:
Fridges in hundreds of French supermarkets heated up to 50°C in one night. The food went in the bin. The attackers never set foot inside. The cooling controls were online, with holes public since 2023.

The heating started on Sunday night, October 11. In some stores it began before midnight. Across France, the systems that keep supermarket fridges cold switched on their defrost function and left it running.

Defrosting is a normal part of how a commercial fridge works. Ice builds up inside, so from time to time the unit warms up to melt it and then goes back to cooling. In these stores that normally adds up to about two hours a day. That night it did not stop. The defrost kept running, and the temperature in display cases and cold rooms kept climbing. One of the chains says the attackers pushed the temperature controls to 50°C, which is 122°F.

Some units ran hot for six hours before staff noticed. In the stores where it started before midnight, the fresh and frozen food had been sitting in that heat for hours by the time the first employees came in. It all had to be thrown out. The Paris prosecutor’s office spoke of a large-scale attack on connected fridges at several big chains, and said it caused food losses and fires.

The chains gave their own numbers. Intermarché counted about 150 of its stores. Thierry Cotillard, head of the group behind it, estimated the losses at tens of millions of euros across the country after a single morning of crisis management. Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were hit. Monoprix put it at about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores. Around 100 stores of Coopérative U, the group behind Super U, Hyper U and U Express, were affected, and its head called the attack “of extreme gravity” and “unprecedented”. Leclerc stores were hit as well.

One store in Alsace lost more than 200,000 euros in food.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu ordered ANSSI, the French national cybersecurity agency, to investigate. France is coordinating with other European countries, because they could be affected too. A threat analyst at the security company Sekoia named Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium as possibly affected, and other reports add the Netherlands to that list.

That same Sunday, Ahold Delhaize, the company behind Albert Heijn, took systems offline after a separate security issue. Its shelves kept showing last week’s prices and online orders stopped. The reports about it do not mention fridges, and so far nothing ties it to the attack in France.

A supermarket has many cooling units, from display cases to cold rooms. Each one has its own small controller. Above those controllers sits one box that ties them together, the system manager. From that box a technician can see the temperature of each unit and change what it is set to. The technician can set up alarms that send an email when something goes wrong, and plan the defrost cycles.

The box has its own web page. A technician opens a browser, types in the address, logs in, and has the store’s cooling on the screen. That way the company that maintains the cooling can check on a store without driving there.

Danfoss, a Danish company, made the boxes in this attack. The models are called the AK-SM and AK-SC series. On October 12, CERT-FR, the French government’s computer emergency team, published an alert saying it knew of many break-ins into boxes from exactly those two series.

The alert also says this: “Exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice.”

To make remote work possible, the web page of the system manager sat straight on the internet, open from outside the store. The login screen answered whoever found it.

Finding it is not hard. Search engines like Shodan and Censys scan the internet day and night. They keep a list of what they see on each address: which ports are open and which software answers on them. In August, security researchers counted 2,765 boxes of the current Danfoss model reachable from the internet.

Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems.” According to the company, most of the units that were hit are old models. The AK-SC355 was phased out in 2016. The AK-SM800 reached its end of life in 2021. The company says these products “no longer receive software or security updates.” The rest were AK-SM 800A units, the current model, running outdated firmware, the software inside the box. It says it has long advised its customers to keep their systems updated. The French retail federation has asked the company for “full transparency”.

For a store, end of life means the box keeps running and keeps controlling the fridges, and no fix will come for it again. The company’s parts are also built into cooling equipment from other manufacturers, and installers can buy them through wholesalers.

The holes in these boxes had been published three times before that Sunday.

The first time was in 2023. On January 18 of that year, researchers reported three flaws in the AK-SM 800A. Danfoss published them on August 21, 2023. The worst one, CVE-2023-25915, let a logged-in user run commands on the box. It scored 9.8 out of 10. Another, CVE-2023-25913, let an outsider pull a report with usernames and store names without logging in. The fix was software version 3.3. That same August the researchers started scanning the internet for vulnerable boxes, and from September 27 they warned the owners they could find.

The second time was in 2025. On March 24, Danfoss warned about a hidden way to log in, CVE-2025-41450. Next to the administrator’s password, the AK-SM 800A accepted a second password, a “code of the day”, calculated from the device’s own date and time. Whoever knows how that calculation works can work out the code and log in without the administrator’s password. The fix was version 4.2.

On August 1, 2025, two more followed. The next hole, CVE-2025-41451, sat in the settings for alarm emails. The box asks for the password of the mail account it uses to send alarms, and that password went into a system command without being checked first. Log in, type the right text into that field, and the box runs it as a command. The other, CVE-2025-41452, let a logged-in user change how the web server inside the box is set up and knock it offline. The fix for both was version 4.3.1. CISA, the US cybersecurity agency, listed these flaws in an advisory.

The third time was on August 9, 2026. Claroty’s Team82, the researchers behind the 2025 flaws, published the full details. They had rebuilt the code-of-the-day calculation. They did not publish it.

That August, the team also published 23 flaws in refrigeration controllers from another maker, Copeland, 21 of them rated high. Some let an attacker take full control of the device without logging in. That maker had fixed them in February.

Two months later, the fridges in France went warm.

French reports say the attackers went after boxes running software older than version 4. That is older than both fixes from 2025. And the two old models get no fixes at all.

The August count covered only the current model, the AK-SM 800A. After the attack, a French tech publication counted nearly 3,000 Danfoss management pages reachable from the internet in France alone. Some of them showed files that were last changed between 2021 and 2024.

How the attackers got in is not known yet. Vincent Strubel, the director of ANSSI, said several vulnerabilities are possible ways in, and that nothing is really established at this stage. So far, the attack is unclaimed.

The attackers may not have needed a known flaw at all. Changing a temperature or a defrost schedule is an ordinary function of the system manager. It is what the web page is for. With a working login, an attacker can change it the same way the technician does, without breaking anything. It is not public whether that login came from a flaw or from a leaked or unchanged password.

That is why the French alert starts with the network. It tells operators to disconnect the AK-SM and AK-SC boxes or filter access to them. Where remote access is essential, it says to limit it to trusted IP addresses for now. If a box may have been broken into, the alert lists six steps:

  • → Restrict network access to the service providers only
  • → Do a factory reset
  • → Apply all available security patches
  • → Change all passwords and keys
  • → Check the existing user accounts
  • → Set the device up again from scratch

Six weeks before France, something with the same pattern happened in the United States.

In the last week of August, refrigeration failed at US military commissaries, the supermarkets on military bases. At least six of them confirmed outages that week, from California to Rhode Island. The agency that runs the commissaries has 235 stores and did not say how many were affected. One of them, Fort Huachuca in Arizona, posted on Facebook that “ALL freezers went into defrost mode” and “ALL frozen food has spoiled.”

The Pentagon said it was aware of “a possible refrigeration disruption at some Defense Commissary Agency commissaries.” It did not name a cause, and it did not say which company made the control systems in those stores. A link between the outages in the US and the attack in France has not been proven. What they share is the pattern: freezers that went into defrost overnight, at that base and in France, and food that was lost by morning.

On September 1, the Army’s cyber investigators and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations confirmed they had opened investigations.

Homes have boxes like this too: a router with remote management switched on, or a camera you can watch from your phone. If one of them answers on the internet, the same search engines find it too.

You can look at your own address the way they do. First find the public IP address of your home connection:

1

curl -4 ifconfig.me

Then open this page, with your own IP address at the end:

1

https://www.shodan.io/host/YOUR-IP-ADDRESS

The -4 makes sure you get your IPv4 address. Shodan shows the ports and services it has seen on that address. If it lists a login page for something in your house, that page can be reached from outside. If your provider shares one address between many customers, which is common with 4G and 5G routers, what Shodan shows is not your house. Do this only for your own address.

What you can do:

  • → Running AK-SM or AK-SC boxes: take them off the internet, or limit access to the address of your maintenance company
  • → AK-SM 800A: update to firmware R4.3.1 or later
  • → AK-SM800 or AK-SC355: these get no updates anymore, and Danfoss advises replacing them
  • → Suspect a compromise: follow the six steps above, starting with a factory reset and new passwords
  • → At home: switch off remote management on your router if you do not use it
  • → Change the default password on anything in your house that has a login page

Want to see what your network shows the internet? Look up your own IP on Shodan, the kind of search that found these controllers. item.title: Ledger Wallet Hidden Spy Chip
item.description:
Crypto worth more than 86 million dollars was drained from Ledger wallets. Each confirmed case was a wallet bought from a shop Ledger had authorized itself. Inside one of them sat a second circuit board.

On October 9, an on-chain investigator who goes by Specter posted a list of ten crypto addresses on X. Ledger users had been reporting empty wallets online, and he followed the stolen funds on Bitcoin, Ethereum and TRON back to where they came from. Money had flowed in from victim wallets, and his count came to more than 86 million dollars. How many wallets that was, he wrote later that day, he could not tell yet.

About an hour later, Ledger posted that it was looking into losses among users in Southeast Asia who had bought their Ledger from one reseller, CryptoBilis. It had asked CryptoBilis to stop selling and shipping Ledger devices. Buyers from the last 90 days were told not to set their device up, and buyers who already had were advised to move their crypto to a new Ledger with a new recovery phrase.

The next day, Ledger wrote: “Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant.” From then on, its advice covered buyers from CryptoBilis whenever they had bought: do not set the device up.

CryptoBilis, an authorized Ledger reseller in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, stopped selling hardware wallets. On October 11, Ledger said the number of affected devices is limited, and that each confirmed case so far is a device sold through CryptoBilis. How much was stolen, Ledger has not confirmed.

A hardware wallet stores the key to your crypto inside a special chip, the secure element, made to resist people who try to pull secrets out of it with lab equipment. When you set the wallet up, it shows you 24 recovery words one time, so you can write them down. With those words, the wallet and the crypto in it can be rebuilt on another device. To show them, the secure element sends them to the small screen. On a Nano X that goes over three thin wires, a connection called the SPI bus, as plain data without any encryption.

Researchers at Tibane Labs tapped those wires on a Nano X themselves while it started up. From the data they caught, they rebuilt the screen exactly as it was drawn, down to the Ledger logo 734.6 milliseconds in. The recovery words travel over the same wires.

The implant is connected to those three wires. It is a small extra board with its own processor, added to a wallet that came out of Ledger’s own factory. Its processor reads along with the screen, picks out the letters and keeps the words. A mobile modem on the same board, with its own SIM card and antenna, then sends them to the attacker. For the owner, nothing changes. item.title: Denmark CPR Breach Took 8.7 Million ID Numbers Through a Two Person Company and the Password 123456
item.description:
8,749,975 Danish ID numbers copied in about ten days. Names and home addresses, the dead included. One company with two employees. Its admin password: 123456. Found only when the invoice came.

The copied data holds names, home addresses and CPR numbers. The CPR number is the personal ID number Danes get at birth, or when they move to the country, and usually keep it for life. People who have died are in the data too, and so are people who moved abroad years ago. Denmark has about 6 million inhabitants. The register behind those numbers holds about 11 million records, and roughly 8.8 million of them were pulled out, according to the Danish digitalisation ministry.

The company the data went through is Pays ApS, a small software firm in Odense. In July 2026 it had two employees, according to the Danish business register. One of its services is what Danes call cpr-vask: cleaning up customer files against the national register, so that names and addresses are up to date.

For that work, the company had legal access to the register. Section 38 of the Danish CPR Act lets private companies look people up when they have a business reason, for example to find the current address of a customer or a member. The law asks the company to have identified each person individually beforehand, by CPR number or by name and address. Banks, telecom companies, insurers, law firms and trade unions have this kind of access. In total, 1,039 organisations do.

The story of how someone else got in comes from a person who says they did it. On Thursday evening, October 8, the Danish newspaper Politiken published its interview with the hacker. The paper spoke to them in English through an encrypted service, and received a file with 8,749,975 CPR records.

Its reporters put a description of the data and the method to several experts, and they all found it very likely that this person took part in the leak. One of them, Emil Hørning of the security company Defend Denmark, called the account credible and the method plausible.

The way in, according to the hacker, was the password of a former employee. That password had leaked earlier, and it was 123456.

The newspaper then did its own checking, and found at least three profiles at the company that used 123456. One of them was the administrator account, the account that can manage the others.

The company’s director and owner confirmed that its legal access to the CPR system had been abused. She declined an interview through her lawyer, and did not answer the newspaper’s questions about the company’s security.

Each lookup in the register costs money, and the CPR office bills the companies for them. On Friday evening, October 2, staff were preparing the invoice for this company. They saw an amount that a department head at the ministry later described at a press briefing as very, very large. Behind it were more than 14 million lookup attempts, made over about ten days in September. The company told the CPR office it had not made those lookups itself.

Documents seen by the Danish broadcaster TV 2 show that the access was in use from September 10. It stayed open for 21 days and 17 hours. The lookups appear to have stopped around September 20. By the time the invoice showed what had happened, whoever made them had been gone for twelve days. Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, said the attacker got what they wanted and then left on their own. He also pointed out that there was no working system to spot the unusual activity.

The register itself is run by DXC Technology, a US company the Danish state hired to operate the CPR register and handle its IT security. The broadcaster has tried to get an answer from the company since October 6, and it has not replied.

14 million attempts against a register of about 11 million records. The ministry’s 8.8 million is the number of lookups that came back with a person. The broadcaster explained the gap: you can also search for numbers that do not exist.

That gap makes sense once you know how a CPR number is built. It has ten digits. The first six are the birth date: day, month, and the last two digits of the year. The seventh digit, read together with the year, tells which century the person was born in. The tenth digit is even for women and odd for men. Statistics Denmark describes the structure in its own documentation of the register.

A person born on 4 March 1985 has a number that starts with 040385. Four more digits follow. For one birth date, that leaves at most 10,000 possible numbers, and many of them were never given to a person. Numbers like that return nothing, which is how a search ends up with more attempts than there are records.

A program that wants most of the register can start from a date instead of a list of names. It tries the possible numbers for that date, keeps the ones that return a person, and moves on to the next day.

In its notice of October 5, the Danish Data Protection Agency writes that the register reported a very large number of automatic lookups, made to find out which CPR numbers are valid. The police have not described the method yet. One detail the hacker gave fits that description too.

AI wrote the program, the hacker told the newspaper. It is more than 40,000 characters long, and two experts who looked at the code for the paper concluded that it was indeed AI-generated. According to the hacker, any AI model launched in the past year could have done it. The hacker denied having strong technical skills.

As an example, the hacker pointed to a bug. The program searched for people born in 1877 instead of 1977, and because of that, people born in 1977 are missing from the file the hacker shared. In a CPR number, 1877 and 1977 have the same first six digits for the same birthday. Only the seventh digit sets the century apart. A program that got the century wrong for one year skipped the Danes born in 1977 who were in the register.

You can change a leaked password in a minute. A CPR number stays. The same documentation says a number is never handed out a second time. Getting a new one is rare. It happens, for example, when the birth date or sex was registered wrong, or after a legal change of gender.

The minister for digitalisation, Christina Egelund, called the breach deeply serious and said it was too early to say whether people will get new numbers. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it was an incident that should not have been possible.

Danes use the CPR number for public services, healthcare, tax and banking. Companies accepted it as a sign that the person on the other side was who they said they were. Laila Reenberg of Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed, the Danish agency for societal security, said you cannot use the number on its own to authorise anything, buy something or get sensitive personal information. She told companies and authorities to stop accepting a CPR number on its own as proof of who someone is.

What the copied data does give a criminal is a convincing start. A phone call or an email from someone who already knows your full name, your address and your ID number sounds like your bank or the tax office. The ministry warned about exactly that on the day it announced the breach. Never give out passwords or other confidential information by phone or email, it said, also when the person seems to know your name, address and CPR number.

Danes took that warning seriously. On October 5, the day the breach was announced, about 1,000 people called the national cyber hotline, against about 150 on a normal day. The government advice site sikkerdigital.dk had 180,000 visits against about 400. A credit warning is a flag that tells lenders to check extra carefully before they give credit in your name. The number of people who had one went from a little under 250,000 on October 1 to about 970,000 on October 7.

On Friday October 9, the CPR office sent a letter to the 1,039 organisations with access. It repeated the security rules they already had to follow. Each needs someone responsible for security and has to check regularly which employees still have access. It also has to keep an eye on how many lookups it makes each month.

Taking that access away is not simple either. The Confederation of Danish Industry, DI, warned that limiting what companies can look up in the register could make their work more expensive and lead to more mistakes. They would have to collect and check the data by hand.

The CPR office has cut off the company’s access and reported the breach to the data protection agency. Officers from the National Unit for Special Crime went to the company on Saturday October 3 to secure evidence, and they are in contact with police abroad. So far there are no charges.

The names and addresses of people with name and address protection are not in the data. MitID, the login Danes use for banks and government services, was not part of this breach. The minister has ordered a full security review of the CPR system.

The hacker told the newspaper that the data will not be sold or published. That is a promise from the person who took it, and nothing more.

123456 keeps showing up. In June I wrote about FortiBleed, where the exact same admin3 account with the password 123456 sat on 2,645 Fortinet firewalls. Pwned Passwords, the list of breached passwords run by Have I Been Pwned, has seen 123456 210,461,208 times.

NIST, the US standards body, tells systems that accept passwords to check each new one against a list of passwords that are common, easy to guess or already leaked. That list is called a blocklist, and the rule is in section 3.1.1.2 of its guideline SP 800-63B-4. A company with access to the register that holds the ID numbers of most of a country had at least three accounts on one of the most common passwords there is.

You can check your own passwords against that same list without sending them anywhere. On Linux, this asks for the password without showing it and turns it into a fixed string of characters that you cannot turn back into the password, a SHA-1 hash. Only the first five characters of that hash go to the service:

1
2
3

printf 'Password: '; read -rs pw; echo
hash=$(printf '%s' "$pw" | sha1sum | awk '{print toupper($1)}'); unset pw
curl -s "https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/${hash:0:5}" | grep "${hash:5}"

The service sends back the hashes that start with those five characters, and grep looks for yours on your own machine. For 123456 the answer is:

1

D09CA3762AF61E59520943DC26494F8941B:210461208

The number after the colon is how often that password was seen in breaches. No output means it is not in the list.

What you can do:

8,749,975 Danish ID numbers copied in about ten days. Names and home addresses, the dead included. One company with two employees. Its admin password: 123456. Found only when the invoice came.

The copied data holds names, home addresses and CPR numbers. The CPR number is the personal ID number Danes get at birth, or when they move to the country, and usually keep it for life. People who have died are in the data too, and so are people who moved abroad years ago. Denmark has about 6 million inhabitants. The register behind those numbers holds about 11 million records, and roughly 8.8 million of them were pulled out, according to the Danish digitalisation ministry.

The company the data went through is Pays ApS, a small software firm in Odense. In July 2026 it had two employees, according to the Danish business register. One of its services is what Danes call cpr-vask: cleaning up customer files against the national register, so that names and addresses are up to date.

For that work, the company had legal access to the register. Section 38 of the Danish CPR Act lets private companies look people up when they have a business reason, for example to find the current address of a customer or a member. The law asks the company to have identified each person individually beforehand, by CPR number or by name and address. Banks, telecom companies, insurers, law firms and trade unions have this kind of access. In total, 1,039 organisations do.

The story of how someone else got in comes from a person who says they did it. On Thursday evening, October 8, the Danish newspaper Politiken published its interview with the hacker. The paper spoke to them in English through an encrypted service, and received a file with 8,749,975 CPR records.

Its reporters put a description of the data and the method to several experts, and they all found it very likely that this person took part in the leak. One of them, Emil Hørning of the security company Defend Denmark, called the account credible and the method plausible.

The way in, according to the hacker, was the password of a former employee. That password had leaked earlier, and it was 123456.

The newspaper then did its own checking, and found at least three profiles at the company that used 123456. One of them was the administrator account, the account that can manage the others.

The company’s director and owner confirmed that its legal access to the CPR system had been abused. She declined an interview through her lawyer, and did not answer the newspaper’s questions about the company’s security.

Each lookup in the register costs money, and the CPR office bills the companies for them. On Friday evening, October 2, staff were preparing the invoice for this company. They saw an amount that a department head at the ministry later described at a press briefing as very, very large. Behind it were more than 14 million lookup attempts, made over about ten days in September. The company told the CPR office it had not made those lookups itself.

Documents seen by the Danish broadcaster TV 2 show that the access was in use from September 10. It stayed open for 21 days and 17 hours. The lookups appear to have stopped around September 20. By the time the invoice showed what had happened, whoever made them had been gone for twelve days. Jens Myrup Pedersen, a cybersecurity professor at Aarhus University, said the attacker got what they wanted and then left on their own. He also pointed out that there was no working system to spot the unusual activity.

The register itself is run by DXC Technology, a US company the Danish state hired to operate the CPR register and handle its IT security. The broadcaster has tried to get an answer from the company since October 6, and it has not replied.

14 million attempts against a register of about 11 million records. The ministry’s 8.8 million is the number of lookups that came back with a person. The broadcaster explained the gap: you can also search for numbers that do not exist.

That gap makes sense once you know how a CPR number is built. It has ten digits. The first six are the birth date: day, month, and the last two digits of the year. The seventh digit, read together with the year, tells which century the person was born in. The tenth digit is even for women and odd for men. Statistics Denmark describes the structure in its own documentation of the register.

A person born on 4 March 1985 has a number that starts with 040385. Four more digits follow. For one birth date, that leaves at most 10,000 possible numbers, and many of them were never given to a person. Numbers like that return nothing, which is how a search ends up with more attempts than there are records.

A program that wants most of the register can start from a date instead of a list of names. It tries the possible numbers for that date, keeps the ones that return a person, and moves on to the next day.

In its notice of October 5, the Danish Data Protection Agency writes that the register reported a very large number of automatic lookups, made to find out which CPR numbers are valid. The police have not described the method yet. One detail the hacker gave fits that description too.

AI wrote the program, the hacker told the newspaper. It is more than 40,000 characters long, and two experts who looked at the code for the paper concluded that it was indeed AI-generated. According to the hacker, any AI model launched in the past year could have done it. The hacker denied having strong technical skills.

As an example, the hacker pointed to a bug. The program searched for people born in 1877 instead of 1977, and because of that, people born in 1977 are missing from the file the hacker shared. In a CPR number, 1877 and 1977 have the same first six digits for the same birthday. Only the seventh digit sets the century apart. A program that got the century wrong for one year skipped the Danes born in 1977 who were in the register.

You can change a leaked password in a minute. A CPR number stays. The same documentation says a number is never handed out a second time. Getting a new one is rare. It happens, for example, when the birth date or sex was registered wrong, or after a legal change of gender.

The minister for digitalisation, Christina Egelund, called the breach deeply serious and said it was too early to say whether people will get new numbers. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it was an incident that should not have been possible.

Danes use the CPR number for public services, healthcare, tax and banking. Companies accepted it as a sign that the person on the other side was who they said they were. Laila Reenberg of Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed, the Danish agency for societal security, said you cannot use the number on its own to authorise anything, buy something or get sensitive personal information. She told companies and authorities to stop accepting a CPR number on its own as proof of who someone is.

What the copied data does give a criminal is a convincing start. A phone call or an email from someone who already knows your full name, your address and your ID number sounds like your bank or the tax office. The ministry warned about exactly that on the day it announced the breach. Never give out passwords or other confidential information by phone or email, it said, also when the person seems to know your name, address and CPR number.

Danes took that warning seriously. On October 5, the day the breach was announced, about 1,000 people called the national cyber hotline, against about 150 on a normal day. item.title: Ahold Delhaize Shut Down Albert Heijn and Five US Chains and Still Will Not Say What Happened
item.description:
77 million shoppers a week. On a Sunday afternoon, the company behind them switched off its own systems. Shelf labels showed last week’s prices. Six days later, it still has not said what happened.

I wrote about this in my newsletter on Friday. This morning, Saturday, the Albert Heijn website still shows an error page. I assume it was an attack. A company that big does not shut everything down for nothing. That is my opinion.

The company is Ahold Delhaize, based in Zaandam in the Netherlands. It owns Albert Heijn in the Netherlands, Delhaize in Belgium, and five chains in the United States. Its own website gives the size: 77 million customers a week, 9,551 stores and 384,000 employees.

On Sunday afternoon, October 11, Albert Heijn and its sister chains Etos and Gall & Gall switched off part of their own computer systems. The company said it did this to protect its IT systems. By Monday morning the website, the app and customer service were offline, and online orders could not be delivered. The personal discounts on the Bonus card stopped working, and so did the savings stamps and Air Miles. The stores stayed open and the tills kept working.

Albert Heijn stores use electronic shelf labels, small screens on the shelf that get their price from a central system. With that system off, the labels kept showing the offers of the week before. At the till, shoppers paid the current price, which was often higher. One store in Amsterdam put up a note to explain it. The labels showed the right prices again on Tuesday, October 13.

The stores get their goods from distribution centres, and those stopped too. At the distribution centre in Tilburg, the workers were sent home around noon on Tuesday. A driver told the regional broadcaster Omroep Brabant: “Nothing works. The systems are down.” Without those systems the staff could not pick the orders for the stores. All Albert Heijn stores in Belgium get their goods from that same centre, the Belgian broadcaster VRT reported, although the chain said the impact in Belgium stayed limited. In the Netherlands, shelves emptied, mostly dairy, vegetables and fruit.

In Belgium, Delhaize customers could not place new online orders, and customer service could not be reached. In the United States, the websites and apps of Food Lion, Stop & Shop, Hannaford, Giant Food and The Giant Company went offline on Monday, October 12. On Wednesday they were still down, and on Friday it was the fifth day in a row. American shoppers were sent to Instacart, DoorDash and Uber Eats instead. A spokesperson for that last chain told the Philadelphia Inquirer that if its app was still down on Friday, it planned to switch on all digital coupons on its customers’ loyalty cards automatically.

Employees felt it too. According to posts from staff on Reddit, quoted by BankInfoSecurity, Stop & Shop workers could not see their schedules or pay stubs in Kronos, their time-tracking system. Food Lion workers lost access to Spectrum, the company’s own platform for picking and handing out online orders. Food Lion staff were told to call it an “IT outage”.

On Monday morning, Ahold Delhaize put out a short press release. It was experiencing “a security issue within its network” and was “taking some systems offline to help protect them”. The same release carried a line meant for investors. It said the release contained news that can move the share price, what EU market rules call inside information. The public got “a security issue”.

On Tuesday, the company said it had “no evidence at this moment” that data of customers, employees or partners was taken, and that it had started to switch some systems back on in a controlled way. In an update on Wednesday, it added that it was working with its own teams, outside cybersecurity experts and the relevant authorities. It would not say more, because that could weaken its security or the way it responds.

In six days, the company has not called it an attack or a hack. Albert Heijn first spoke of an IT incident, and later of a cybersecurity incident.

On Tuesday, the public broadcaster NOS spoke to anonymous people in the security sector. According to them, the security staff at Albert Heijn saw suspicious attack traffic coming in, and switched the systems off while it was arriving. That, they said, stopped the attackers from getting deeper into the network. The traffic came through servers in the United States, Poland, Moldova and Turkey. Servers of Ahold’s own American branch may have been used as well, but that is not confirmed. Albert Heijn did confirm one thing: it shared details about the servers the attackers used with other companies.

Attackers rent servers in whatever country they like, or break into someone else’s server and send their traffic through it. A server in Poland shows the route the traffic took, and nothing about where the attackers are. The broadcaster made the same point. In cybersecurity, attribution, working out who is behind an attack, is one of the hardest problems.

Pim Takkenberg is a security specialist and a former police officer. On the current affairs programme Nieuwsuur he said: “It seems pretty clear to me that someone with bad intentions has been inside the system.” He thinks of criminals who are after money. He also told the broadcaster that the attackers may have broken into the American servers first, and attacked the Dutch systems from there.

On Friday, November 8, 2024, the American branch of Ahold Delhaize announced that it had detected a cybersecurity issue in its US network. It took some systems offline “to help protect them”. Hannaford stopped pickup and delivery orders for several days. The company said it had brought in outside cybersecurity experts and notified law enforcement.

Five months later, on April 16, 2025, the ransomware group INC Ransom put Ahold Delhaize on its leak site, a website where criminals publish what they stole from companies that do not pay. The group claimed up to 6 terabytes of stolen data. One day later, the company confirmed that files from its American systems had been stolen.

In June 2025, a notice filed with the US state of Maine put the number of people at more than 2.2 million. They were current and former staff and their family members. Depending on the person, the files held names, contact details and dates of birth, Social Security, passport and driver’s license numbers, bank account numbers and health information. In July 2025, one of them filed a class action against the company, a lawsuit on behalf of a large group of affected people, in a federal court in North Carolina.

The stolen files were not only about Americans. In April 2025, Ahold Delhaize said it suspected that data of staff in the Netherlands had been taken as well. It concerned people on the payroll in April 2021 at Albert Heijn, Etos, Gall & Gall and other parts of the group. According to the newspaper AD, that meant names, bank account numbers and the amount of their salary payment of early April 2021. Ahold reported it to the Dutch Data Protection Authority. This week, the anonymous sources pointed to servers of that same American branch.

Same company, same words, almost two years apart. Last time, the full picture came out five months later, after the criminals had put it on their own leak site.

A company can have reasons to say little while an investigation runs. A public statement can come back later in a lawsuit, or in the claim with an insurer, and since 2025 Ahold knows the first one from experience. Whether that is the reason now, the company has not said.

The Dutch police and the Public Prosecution Service did something unusual on Wednesday, October 14. They publicly invited Ahold to file a police report. Police rarely do that in public, the broadcaster noted.

Ahold did report the incident to the National Cyber Security Centre, as a new Dutch cyber law that took effect in August requires. That notice is not the same as a report to the police.

The police and prosecutors can also start an investigation on their own, without a report. They have not. Stan Duijf, who leads the police approach to cybercrime, explained why on the talk show Pauw & De Wit on Thursday. Albert Heijn says no sensitive customer data was lost, and he called that an important reason not to start one yet. He also said: “We say: do it as early as possible, because then we can actively start the investigation.”

The police call the first hours after an attack the golden hour. The longer it takes before investigators can start, the more traces disappear. With an investigation, the police can seize servers or search them to see what runs on an IP address.

In 2024, the American branch notified law enforcement from the start. This time, in the Netherlands, the police are relying on the company’s own word.

By Thursday evening, the company had still not filed a police report. On Friday, justice minister David van Weel said he understood that a company first focuses on protecting its systems, but that the time had come to file a report. He was also in contact with Frans Muller, the CEO of Ahold Delhaize, and pressed him for openness. A spokesperson said they could not respond to the minister’s words, Reuters reported.

Three estimates of the damage are going around, and they are far apart.

Cor Molenaar, emeritus professor of e-marketing at Erasmus University Rotterdam, put the damage for Albert Heijn at about 10 million euros, and warned it could grow fast the longer it lasts. He also thinks it was a DDoS attack, where many computers flood a system with traffic until it stops working. The other experts I found think someone got inside.

Retail expert Erik Hemmes calculated that Albert Heijn had missed about 21 million euros in revenue in its stores and online by Wednesday.

The financial paper Het Financieele Dagblad heard from people in the supermarket sector, who did not want to be named, that the crisis costs Ahold Delhaize tens of millions of euros a day. Ahold told that paper it was too early to say what the financial impact would be.

For scale: in the last three months of 2025, Ahold Delhaize sold for 23.5 billion euros. That is more than 250 million euros a day, for all of Ahold Delhaize together. Most of it comes through the tills in the stores, and those stayed open. Shoppers who could not order from Albert Heijn went elsewhere. Jumbo, Lidl, Picnic, ALDI and PLUS all told the news agency ANP that their stores were busier and they got more online orders.

On the stock market, the share fell almost 3 percent on Monday, the biggest loser in the Amsterdam AEX index that day, and then recovered. It closed at 32.36 euros on Friday. On November 4, Ahold Delhaize publishes its results for the third quarter, its first scheduled results since the incident started.

That same Sunday night, a few hours after the systems at Albert Heijn went off, attackers heated the fridges and freezers in hundreds of French supermarkets to 50°C. I wrote about that on Tuesday. Two incidents at supermarket groups in one weekend, and yet Ahold Delhaize and the NCSC both said they see no sign that the two are connected.

An intrusion into a company network usually starts at one weak point: a stolen password, or a server facing the internet that missed an update. The password often comes from a phishing email that tricks an employee into typing it on a fake page. From that first machine, the attacker looks around, to see which other machines are on the network and where the passwords are kept. The attacker collects those passwords and moves from machine to machine, until reaching the systems that run the business or hold the data.

In a ransomware attack, the data gets copied out first. Then the attacker encrypts the files on the machines, so the company cannot open them. The company now has two reasons to pay: to get its systems back, and to keep its data off a leak site.

This is why security staff pull systems off the network the moment they see attack traffic. An attacker sitting on one machine needs the network to reach the next one. Cut the connections, and the attacker is stuck. The company is stuck too. At Albert Heijn the tills kept working, but the distribution centres, the app and the deliveries did not. Days of empty shelves and more than a week of cancelled orders are the price of not letting someone go further. The company says it has no evidence so far that anything was taken.

As of Friday evening, Albert Heijn had cancelled all online orders up to and including Tuesday, October 20, and new orders still could not be placed. Customers who already paid will be compensated once the systems work again. Deliveries should start again in the second half of next week. Customer service is still unreachable. The shelves are full again.

On November 4 the company talks to its investors. Until then, a leak site may say more than Ahold Delhaize does.
