A company can have reasons to say little while an investigation runs. A public statement can come back later in a lawsuit, or in the claim with an insurer, and since 2025 Ahold knows the first one from experience. Whether that is the reason now, the company has not said.

The Dutch police and the Public Prosecution Service did something unusual on Wednesday, October 14. They publicly invited Ahold to file a police report. Police rarely do that in public, the broadcaster noted.

Ahold did report the incident to the National Cyber Security Centre, as a new Dutch cyber law that took effect in August requires. That notice is not the same as a report to the police.

The police and prosecutors can also start an investigation on their own, without a report. They have not. Stan Duijf, who leads the police approach to cybercrime, explained why on the talk show Pauw & De Wit on Thursday. Albert Heijn says no sensitive customer data was lost, and he called that an important reason not to start one yet. He also said: “We say: do it as early as possible, because then we can actively start the investigation.”

The police call the first hours after an attack the golden hour. The longer it takes before investigators can start, the more traces disappear. With an investigation, the police can seize servers or search them to see what runs on an IP address.

In 2024, the American branch notified law enforcement from the start. This time, in the Netherlands, the police are relying on the company’s own word.

By Thursday evening, the company had still not filed a police report. On Friday, justice minister David van Weel said he understood that a company first focuses on protecting its systems, but that the time had come to file a report. He was also in contact with Frans Muller, the CEO of Ahold Delhaize, and pressed him for openness. A spokesperson said they could not respond to the minister’s words, Reuters reported.

Three estimates of the damage are going around, and they are far apart.

Cor Molenaar, emeritus professor of e-marketing at Erasmus University Rotterdam, put the damage for Albert Heijn at about 10 million euros, and warned it could grow fast the longer it lasts. He also thinks it was a DDoS attack, where many computers flood a system with traffic until it stops working. The other experts I found think someone got inside.

Retail expert Erik Hemmes calculated that Albert Heijn had missed about 21 million euros in revenue in its stores and online by Wednesday.

The financial paper Het Financieele Dagblad heard from people in the supermarket sector, who did not want to be named, that the crisis costs Ahold Delhaize tens of millions of euros a day. Ahold told that paper it was too early to say what the financial impact would be.

For scale: in the last three months of 2025, Ahold Delhaize sold for 23.5 billion euros. That is more than 250 million euros a day, for all of Ahold Delhaize together. Most of it comes through the tills in the stores, and those stayed open. Shoppers who could not order from Albert Heijn went elsewhere. Jumbo, Lidl, Picnic, ALDI and PLUS all told the news agency ANP that their stores were busier and they got more online orders.

On the stock market, the share fell almost 3 percent on Monday, the biggest loser in the Amsterdam AEX index that day, and then recovered. It closed at 32.36 euros on Friday. On November 4, Ahold Delhaize publishes its results for the third quarter, its first scheduled results since the incident started.

That same Sunday night, a few hours after the systems at Albert Heijn went off, attackers heated the fridges and freezers in hundreds of French supermarkets to 50°C. I wrote about that on Tuesday. Two incidents at supermarket groups in one weekend, and yet Ahold Delhaize and the NCSC both said they see no sign that the two are connected.

An intrusion into a company network usually starts at one weak point: a stolen password, or a server facing the internet that missed an update. From that first machine, the attacker looks around, to see which other machines are on the network and where the passwords are kept. item.title: LG Smart TVs Could Be Taken Over From the Same WiFi Without a PIN
item.description:
Three bugs chained in order gave an attacker full control of a smart TV, straight over the home WiFi, without the set ever asking for its PIN. The owner did nothing wrong. A demo app that ships on the TV, and a test certificate it still trusted, were enough to reach root.

Root is the account that sits above everything else on the machine. With it you can read what is on the TV, change any setting, install software, and switch the hardware on and off.

The person who got there did not touch the remote and did not know the owner’s account. What they needed was a place on the same network. A guest who got the WiFi password once, a phone in the house with a bad app on it, or a laptop that was already infected. Any of those is close enough.

A smart TV sits in the corner and plays Netflix. Underneath it is a computer with its own operating system, and it can be attacked like any other.

LG calls that system webOS. By the company’s own count it runs on more than 200 million LG televisions. This attack was built and shown on two of them.

An independent researcher showed it at TyphoonPWN 2026, a live hacking contest in Seoul run by a company called SSD Secure Disclosure. At a contest like this, a researcher brings a working attack, runs it on stage against the device, and gets paid if it lands. The prize pool reaches into the hundreds of thousands of dollars.

This one took third place in the LG category. The researcher chose to stay anonymous, and the full writeup went public on October 12.

It was tested on two sets, the LG 32LQ636BPSA and the 27TQ600SW. Both ran webOS 7.5.7-25 on firmware 04.54.40. They are small sets, a 32-inch and a 27-inch, the kind that end up in a kitchen or a bedroom. How far it reaches past those two, the research does not say.

Start with how the TV is supposed to stay safe.

To run the TV from your phone, you use LG’s ThinQ app, and the two have to be introduced first. The TV shows a code on the screen. You type that code into the phone. Only then does the TV trust it.

That on-screen code does one job: it proves the phone is in the same room as the person with the remote, and not someone sitting out on the network.

webOS also keeps its apps apart, so a small app cannot reach in and call the services that run the television. Three mistakes take all of that apart, one after the other.

The first mistake is about that code.

These TVs ship with a small built-in app called sync-demo. It is the kind of app that runs on a demo set in a shop. Inside it sits a pairing file, signed by LG itself so the TV knows it is genuine.

The attacker copies that signed file and sends it to the part of the TV that handles pairing. Two things go wrong at the same time.

The file asks for a permission called STB_INTERNAL_CONNECTION. The TV reads that as a connection it already trusts from the inside, so it decides no code needs to be shown.

Someone signed that file with a test certificate, the kind developers use on the workbench. A TV in a living room should never have trusted it. This one did.

So the TV skips the code and hands back a key at its highest level of trust.

One key is not full control yet. The second mistake widens the opening.

Another built-in app, cmp-client, can be told to open a web page. It takes the address of that page from whoever starts it.

Before it opens the page, it runs one weak check. It asks the address whether it is there, and if it answers, the app loads it. It never checks where the address actually points.

So the attacker points it at a page of their own.

What makes this serious is where that page runs. It runs inside a trusted app, and it keeps that app’s line to the services deep inside the TV. A web page the attacker wrote can now call controls that an outside connection is never allowed to touch.

The third mistake runs the command.

The TV has a service that collects log files, called pmlogd. One of its jobs asks for the name of a folder to put the logs in, and it builds a system command out of whatever name it is handed. It drops that name into the command without cleaning it first.

Send it an ordinary folder name and nothing happens. Send it a folder name with an extra command added on, and the TV runs the extra command too.

pmlogd runs as root. So the command runs as root.

Put the three together and the path is short: skip the code, reach the service that was supposed to be out of reach, and run a command as the most powerful user on the machine. The researcher’s proof ends with the TV printing uid=0. That is the system’s own way of saying you are root.

A rooted TV is a foothold inside the house.

From there an attacker can look across the home network and find the router, the laptops, the phones and the other smart gadgets, and go after those too. They can leave their own software on the set, quiet and out of sight, and use the TV as one more machine in a botnet that attacks other people. They can reach the accounts you signed into on the set.

Earlier work on webOS by security researchers listed the same risks: move sideways through the network, pull the TV into a botnet, or watch the owner.

Most of the news stopped at one line: three bugs, no CVE. LG’s own security bulletin tells more.

In its September update, labelled SMR-SEP-2026, LG lists five problems, not three. LG rates all five High. All five landed on the same day, June 18, 2026, and LG credits them to SSD Secure Disclosure.

Three of them are the ones in the public writeup: the hard-coded secret in sync-demo, the weak address check in cmp-client, and the command injection in pmlogd.

The other two never made the writeup. One is a way past the login check in the second-screen gateway service. The other lets an attacker gain higher rights through the first-time setup screen.

So “no CVE” is true in one narrow way. These did not get numbers from MITRE, the body that hands out CVE numbers. In any practical way it is wrong. LG runs its own list, which it calls LVE, and on that list the flaws were logged, numbered and fixed.

One detail is easy to miss.

That second-screen gateway service, the one with the login bypass on this year’s list, is the same service Bitdefender broke in 2024. Back then, one of their bugs, CVE-2023-6317, slipped past the security PIN in that service and created a privileged account with no action from the owner. A second, CVE-2023-6318, ran commands as root.

Two years later, a different team, the same two moves: get past the check that proves you belong, then run a command as root. The service even carries the same name.

That 2024 round was not small either. The firm found four flaws across webOS versions 4 through 7. When they searched Shodan, the search engine for devices connected to the internet, they counted more than 91,000 TVs with the weak service open to the public internet. It was only ever meant for the home network.

LG fixed those in 2024. And it keeps happening at this one contest. A year earlier, at TyphoonPWN 2025, another researcher took first place in the LG category with a different chain. That one walked out of a folder it was locked into and read the stored keys of phones that had paired with the TV.

The living-room set has become a regular target in Seoul.

The limits matter too. Only those two sets were tested, so how far the chain reaches across other webOS 7.5 models is not something the research settles.

The attacker has to be on the same network as the TV. Someone has to be past the router already, on a network the TV trusts by default. The open internet does not reach it directly.

And LG has pushed a fix, on its TV security bulletin page. A set that is up to date, and off the affected firmware, is not open to this chain.

LG says it sends security updates to a webOS platform for five years after that platform first ships. A set older than that window eventually drops off the list, which is worth checking if the TV in the room has a few years on it.

What you can do:

  • → Update your TV’s firmware now, and turn on automatic updates so the next fix arrives on its own
  • → Look at what is connected to your home WiFi, and drop anything you do not recognise
  • → Put your smart TV and other smart-home gear on a separate guest network, away from your phone and your computer
  • → Treat the local network as something that can be reached; a guest’s phone sits on it too
  • → If a TV does not need the internet for what you watch on it, there is no harm in taking it off the network
  • → In the TV’s settings, turn off the microphone and voice features if you do not use them

item.title: Discover-Tech Ads Delivered Zero-Click Spyware to Al Jazeera While Google Approved the Company for Six Years
item.description:
Spyware got onto Al Jazeera devices through an ad that only had to load on the screen. 45 were targeted, and the owners did nothing wrong. The company behind the ad ran code on 120,768 websites, approved by Google for six years.

On October 15, two teams published the same finding on the same day. Researchers at the Citizen Lab in Toronto and the ad-security company Confiant laid out the first clear proof of something security people had warned about for years: spyware that lands on a phone or a laptop through an ordinary online ad. There was no link to click and no file to download. They gave it a name, AdFection.

The usual warning is about shady links you should not click. This one had nothing to click. The ad only had to appear on the screen. The moment it loaded, a small piece of code inside it reached out to a server and asked one question: is this the person we are looking for? If the answer was yes, the attack ran. If the answer was no, the server sent back nothing, and the reader scrolled on, never knowing an ad had checked who they were.

The company at the center of this is Discover-Tech, an Israeli firm registered in 2020. On paper it looked like any other advertising business. The books say otherwise. In four months it spent only about 109,000 dollars, the records show almost no income from selling ads, and more than a third of its budget went to promoting its own website.

It bought ad space in the same automated auctions that fund most of the free internet. And it was trusted. From 2020 until this month, Discover-Tech sat on the lists of certified and approved ad vendors kept by Google and by IAB Europe, the trade body for the industry. For six years this was a vendor in good standing. Google cut its access in early October and said it did so “for systematically violating our policies.” The trade body dropped it around the same time.

To see how an ad can carry an attack, it helps to know what happens in the half second before any ad appears. When a page or an app opens a slot for an ad, it does not pick one in advance. It holds an auction. Dozens of companies get told what device you are on and where you are, tagged with a code called your advertising ID that follows you from app to app. They bid, live, for the right to show you something. The highest bid wins, and its ad drops into the slot. This happens hundreds of billions of times a day, and it is over before the page has even settled.

Discover-Tech bid in these auctions like any other buyer. But some of the ads it won carried something extra. The instant the ad rendered, a line of code phoned home to a Discover-Tech server and handed over your advertising ID and IP address, along with the cookies on the page. The server checked those details against a target list. If your device was not on it, the reply was exactly zero bytes. If it was, you got a block of code that ran on the spot. Because the server stayed silent for the rest, the scanners that are supposed to catch bad ads had nothing to flag.

The targeting was a product, not a one-off. On Discover-Tech’s platform a customer could pick a single person by advertising ID, by browser, or by IP address, and push a chosen ad straight to that one device. Clients could run it under their own branding and limit a campaign to a single country.

The scale is the part that is hard to sit with. Between March and June of this year, the researchers counted Discover-Tech bidding on 3.77 billion ad slots and winning about 442 million. Ads carrying its code showed up in 75,373 apps and on 120,768 websites, across 161 countries. At least 718 million of those bids carried the hidden code that calls home.

The heaviest targeting landed on conflict zones and small states. Yemen drew 457 million bids. In Montenegro the ads were aimed at people more than 150 times over, counted per head of population. Confiant’s cofounder Jerome Dangu put it at 10 million ads a day, and said very likely hundreds of millions of people were touched by Discover-Tech. In the Palestinian territories, he said, the ads were hard to avoid. Most of those ads were ordinary. But the same channel that carried a harmless Sudoku ad to one phone carried spyware to a target on another, and from the outside the two looked the same.

It was not only far away. In the Netherlands, 1 in 54 ads shown on iPhones came from Discover-Tech. Belgium was the single most-targeted country Confiant counted, 56 percent of all the hits, first seen on April 12.

A second trick makes it worse. Ad companies swap data with each other through something called cookie matching, a quiet arrangement that lets them recognize the same person across different sites. Discover-Tech could even follow people onto sites where its own ads never ran. Once you are in the system, stepping out of it is not up to you.

The proof that this was more than theory came from Al Jazeera. The network’s own technology team noticed odd patterns on some journalists’ devices back in 2024, and the pattern kept running into 2025. They brought in the Citizen Lab. The investigators found at least 45 devices inside the network had been targeted, and confirmed that some were infected. The logs showed the same sequence: first contact with a Discover-Tech ad server, then a check-in with a second server, then the device talking to the machine that runs the spyware. The team pulled one infected Windows file off a device. It survives a reboot by editing a Windows setting so it loads again each time the machine boots.

The spyware itself was made by Candiru, an Israeli company that sells surveillance tools only to governments. The name is not new. In July 2021, security researchers and Microsoft mapped its work and found at least 100 victims, among them journalists, activists and dissidents, plus two holes in Windows that got patched. That November, the US government put the company on a trade blacklist, the list of firms American companies may not export to without a special license. It now calls itself Integrity Labs. Its spyware can take files, read messages, log what you type, switch on the microphone and camera, and grab screenshots.

The find that says the most about this operation is almost dull. Discover-Tech left an open page on the internet, no password, holding 128 days of sign-in records. It showed who had been signing in to the targeting platform: 120 different usernames. Two were tied to Candiru, and those two signed in from eight countries, among them the United States, Italy and the Czech Republic. And until March of this year, one of the company’s shareholders was linked to Sara Hamou. She ran the corporate network behind Intellexa, the group behind the Predator spyware, and was convicted in Greece in the case known as Predatorgate. These are not separate worlds. They overlap.

The ads did not only reach journalists. The researchers found Discover-Tech impressions inside the networks of the Norwegian parliament, the Norwegian police, the European Parliament, the European Commission, NATO and the UN. They also found ads inside the networks of 19 media organisations across eight countries. Confiant saw them on networks tied to the Pentagon, the UN’s atomic agency, and the International Criminal Court. One caution here: an ad showing up on a network is not the same as a device being infected. It means the door was knocked on, not that someone walked through. But it shows how far the reach went.

And most of the ads tied to Candiru did not land on government networks at all. They landed on ordinary home and mobile connections, in living rooms. Whoever sat in their database could be reached on their own phone, whatever network they used.

The spyware was not the only thing these ads carried. item.title: Siemens Software Center Ran Attackers' Code With a Valid Siemens Signature on PCs That Never Installed It
item.description:
Canon, then Stardock, now Siemens. Attackers keep running their code behind a trusted signature. On October 19 Siemens confirmed its own signed program was the latest, on Windows PCs that never had it.

Here is what it looked like on a PC that got hit. A program called Siemens Software Center, sitting in the list of apps that start with Windows. On a machine that never had Siemens software on it. The owner did not put it there. It loaded on its own at startup.

That program is genuine. Siemens makes it, and its customers use it to download, install and update the software they bought from Siemens. It even carries Siemens’ own digital signature, which tells Windows “we made this file, and it has not been changed.” Both of those things were true here. The file was genuine. The signature checked out. And it was running the attacker’s code.

Siemens confirmed all of this on October 19.

So how does a genuine, signed program end up on a machine that never asked for it, running someone else’s code? It takes two steps, and I will walk through both.

The first step is how it landed on the computer at all. The trick is called ClickFix, and I wrote about it on October 3. It goes like this. You open a web page, and the page tells you something needs to be verified or fixed. It asks you to press Win+R, paste in a line it gives you, and hit Enter. What you cannot see is that the page already dropped a command onto your clipboard. Win+R opens the little Run box in Windows, the one that runs whatever you put in it.

You think you are proving you are human. In that one paste, you run the attacker’s command, on your own PC, with your own account.

That is why the Siemens warning carries one line meant for ordinary people and not for IT staff: never paste a command from a web page into Win+R, the Run box or PowerShell.

That pasted command pulled in an installer called AllMyBasic.msi from a server the attackers controlled. The installer made a folder named SM Software Provisioning Service in a corner of the user’s own account, and dropped the original SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe inside it. Right next to that file it placed its own, among them one called archive.dll. Then it gave the program a spot in the startup apps, so it comes back after a reboot.

And that one extra file, lying beside the original one, is the attack itself. To see why, you need one small thing about how Windows programs are put together.

A program is almost never a single file. Around the main program sit smaller helper files, called DLLs, that hold pieces of the code the program leans on while it runs. When the program needs one, it asks Windows for it by name. Windows then looks in a fixed order, and the first folder it checks is the one the program was started from. The first file it finds with the right name wins. It does not ask who made it.

So the attackers gave their file the name the program was looking for and left it in that same folder. The program asked for its helper, grabbed the attacker’s file instead, and ran it. There was no warning. The security world calls this DLL sideloading. Siemens logged it as CVE-2026-110936, in the family of bugs known as an uncontrolled search path.

The signature on SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe vouches for that one file, and nothing else. It says Siemens made it and it was not tampered with, and that stayed true throughout. It says nothing about archive.dll sitting beside it. So the moment the program loaded that DLL, the attacker’s code was running inside a process Windows saw as trusted Siemens software. That is exactly why they picked this program. Siemens said so plainly: they chose it because it is signed and trusted.

On paper the bug does not even look frightening. Siemens scores it 8.4 out of 10 on the newer scale and 6.7 on the older one, and the fine print assumes the attacker is already on your machine with high rights, ready to drop that DLL. But in these attacks the person dropping the DLL is you, by pasting the one command that brought it in.

Siemens is not the first brand used this way, and the warning was already out there.

On September 28, researchers at Huntress laid out a run of attacks that, for some victims, began with a Google search for the word chatgpt. A paid result at the top pointed to a custom assistant hosted on the genuine chatgpt.com. Talk to it, and it gave the same answer each time: the service is busy, please use our backup page. The backup page was a fake Cloudflare check, and the check asked you to paste a command. The same ClickFix move.

That command installed a fake printer tool built around a genuine program signed by Canon, and used it to sideload the attacker’s DLL, the same trick used on Siemens. A later wave swapped Canon for a program signed by Stardock. Both ended in the same place: a remote access tool that hands over the screen, the camera and the microphone, and comes with a file manager that searches through the contents of the files on the PC. Huntress counted at least 40 incidents.

And they do not sit still. The first fake assistant came down on September 25. Two days later there was a new one. By October 14 they had fresh web addresses in rotation, like gptverification[.]com. Take one down, another is already up.

In that same report, back in September, the researchers wrote plainly that it was highly likely other signed programs were being abused the same way, and that any alarm built on those two names would miss the next one. Three weeks later, the next one carried a Siemens signature. And the Siemens flaw was reported to the company by Jose Oregon of Huntress Labs, from the same team behind that report.

The second connection comes from Forescout. On October 15, the same day the Siemens advisory came out, its researchers published a write-up of something called ROMULUS. They had been working a separate case and noticed the malware was coming from a server running a login panel by that name. ROMULUS turned out to be a ready-made delivery system for ClickFix attacks: one web address hands a victim a PowerShell script, another hands over an installer, and on one of the servers a stats page quietly counted installs and runs by country.

They found it on six servers. One of them, 2.27.248[.]127, is the exact server Siemens named as the one that handed out the AllMyBasic.msi bundle with the signed program inside. Another, 96.62.224[.]81, is the one behind the fake chatgpt assistant. The same servers, three different signed brands.

Who runs ROMULUS is still an open question. Forescout is careful about it: it could be one private crew, a service other criminals rent, an affiliate setup, or a tool that got copied around. What we can be sure of is how the malware works and which server sent it, not who is behind it.

This is also not the first time Siemens Software Center had a DLL problem. Back in August 2023, Siemens disclosed the same class of flaw in the same program, CVE-2021-41544, reported by a researcher at Dragos and fixed in version 3.0. Three years on, the same weakness turned up again in a newer version, 3.5.8.7, and this time someone put it to use.

On October 17 Siemens added the fix, version 4.0.9.8, to its advisory. If you already run Siemens Software Center for work, you do not have to do anything, because it updates itself the next time you open it. That closes the hole for the people who actually use the program.

It does nothing about the copy the attackers carry. Their bundle brings its own old 3.5.8.7, with the genuine signature still on it, drops it in its own folder, and never goes near Siemens’ official download. Siemens has said nothing about pulling back the certificate behind that signature. Its own advice points the same way: do not rely on the file’s fingerprint, because the file is Siemens’ own and the fingerprint matches. Watch the folders and the behaviour instead.

Siemens lists these signs of trouble, for users and for defenders:

  • → Siemens Software Center in your startup apps or Task Scheduler on a PC that never had it installed
  • → A folder called SM Software Provisioning Service in AppData\Local\Programs
  • → SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe running from AppData\Local\Programs, started by msiexec
  • → The files activate.bak or statinfosta.DB next to SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe
  • → A folder called FTSuite with a file called ftc.uml in AppData\Local
  • → Connections to 96.62.218[.]59

You can check the two folders yourself in PowerShell, run as the user who might have pasted the command:

1
2
3
4

Test-Path "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\SM Software Provisioning Service"
Test-Path "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\FTSuite\ftc.uml"
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object { $_.TaskName -like "*Siemens*" }
Get-CimInstance Win32_StartupCommand | Where-Object { $_.Command -like "*Siemens*" }

The two Test-Path lines answer True or False. A True on either one, or a Siemens entry in the last two lines on a PC with no Siemens software, means the machine needs a closer look.

For the people who run the network, Siemens gives the indicators to block and to search the logs for:

1
2
3
4

Active:   96.62.218[.]59 and wizardexpensive[.]com (payload hosting and C2)
Inactive: 2.27.248[.]127 (distributed AllMyBasic.msi)
AllMyBasic.msi  SHA-256 f4d7c5321bb0d1bda439304a753bcf9b467b98ca53c7e9493b9c2c3451092e4a
archive.dll     SHA-256 3fdcc7d7d049a89711fb31fb236940a1c5a09d899143ffd20c3c41fb1f2cf491

The inactive server is down now, but a machine that pulled from it earlier can still be infected. Siemens also says to look for unexpected DLLs next to Siemens programs outside the normal install folder.

If a PC matches, Siemens says to take it off the network, stop the process, remove the startup entry and the scheduled task, and reset the passwords, before the usual incident response. Change the passwords used on that machine first, from a different device.

Siemens says it knows of no break-in to its own systems, products or update channels, and that the attackers spread the signed program together with their own files outside the official channels. The company is sharing what it knows with the authorities and with security vendors. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security put out its own warning, AV26-1063, the same day. There are no victim numbers, and no name has been put to the attackers.

A signature covers one file, the one it is attached to. It says nothing about the other files that program pulls in while it runs.

Want to see what is starting up on your own Windows machine, and spot the one entry that does not belong? That begins with understanding how programs load and where things hide. Siemens lists these signs of trouble, for users and for defenders:

  • → Siemens Software Center in your startup apps or Task Scheduler on a PC that never had it installed
  • → A folder called SM Software Provisioning Service in AppData\Local\Programs
  • → SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe running from AppData\Local\Programs, started by msiexec
  • → The files activate.bak or statinfosta.DB next to SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe
  • → A folder called FTSuite with a file called ftc.uml in AppData\Local
  • → Connections to 96.62.218[.]59

The inactive server is down now, but a machine that pulled from it earlier can still be infected. Siemens also says to look for unexpected DLLs next to Siemens programs outside the normal install folder.

If a PC matches, Siemens says to take it off the network, stop the process, remove the startup entry and the scheduled task, and reset the passwords, before the usual incident response. Change the passwords used on that machine first, from a different device.

Siemens says it knows of no break-in to its own systems, products or update channels, and that the attackers spread the signed program together with their own files outside the official channels. The company is sharing what it knows with the authorities and with security vendors. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security put out its own warning, AV26-1063, the same day. There are no victim numbers, and no name has been put to the attackers.

A signature covers one file, the one it is attached to. It says nothing about the other files that program pulls in while it runs.
